summary.oneLiner: Shree Cement Limited is an integrated Indian cement manufacturer that describes itself as one of the lowest-cost cement producers in the industry, operating 69.30 MTPA of cement capacity (63.3 MTPA standalone) as of 31st March, 2026.
summary.business: The Company manufactures and sells clinker, cement and Ready Mix Concrete (RMC), which together account for 95.05% of turnover under NIC codes 2394 and 2395. It operates 6 integrated cement unit locations, 10 grinding unit locations and 26 RMC units in India, supported by captive power including waste heat recovery and renewables. It serves a diverse customer base spanning institutional clients and retail consumers, supplying cement for projects ranging from large-scale infrastructure to individual housing units.

currentContext.strengths: Cost leadership: sustained focus on optimising raw material, energy, logistics and fuel costs means the Company 'is widely recognised as one of the lowest-cost cement producers in the industry'|Premium product mix: ratio of premium products to total trade sales improved from 14.9% in 2024-25 to 20.8% in 2025-26|Distribution and brand: continued emphasis on brand building, strengthening and expanding the dealer and distribution network, the 'Club Royal' dealer loyalty programme, IPL franchise sponsorship and an always-on television campaign|Customer franchise: 71% of revenue from repeat customers and a 91% customer satisfaction score|Energy self-supply and green power: 634.50 MW green energy capacity and 62.1% share of green electricity in total electricity consumption, supporting cost control|Scale and integration: capacity built from 25.60 MTPA (31st March, 2016) to 69.30 MTPA (31st March, 2026) alongside power capacity of 1,137.50 MW|Innovation capability: 5 patents granted, Rs 28.51 Crore total R&D investment and DSIR-approved R&D labs at 4 locations|Logistics optimisation through demand-aligned dispatch locations, IT-enabled analytics, digital route optimisation and deployment of electric vehicles for cement deliveries
currentContext.strategies: Strategic priority S1 - Cost leadership through efficiency and energy transition; strategic priority S3 - Sustainable growth through cleaner, smarter expansion|Disciplined capacity expansion and integrated operations: multiple potential locations for integrated and grinding units are evaluated with a focus on proximity to key markets and access to optimal limestone reserves, supported by in-house land, commercial and engineering teams and by monitoring limestone auction opportunities|Faster stabilisation and ramp-up of newly commissioned plants to rated capacity, integrating best-in-class high-efficiency technologies to minimise typical ramp-up timelines (Jaitaran and Kodla optimised within a fortnight)|Standardisation and replication across plants - once an operational improvement is validated at one plant it is systematically implemented across the network|RMC as a downstream extension of manufacturing: co-located plants for supply-chain efficiency, with the aim of expanding the footprint in the upcoming years to become a significant player in the RMC segment|Energy leadership through an integrated power portfolio combining thermal, renewable and waste heat recovery, with a long-term direction of near self-sufficiency in power consumption|Increasing use of alternative fuels and raw materials, backed by investment in equipment able to handle varied and complex wastes, given their substantial cost advantage over conventional fuels|Cost as a structural discipline: with fuel and power accounting for nearly 70% of clinker costs, continuous lowering of variable costs through process optimisation, lower clinker factors and greater use of alternative raw materials and fuels|Mining excellence as a competitive differentiator - GPS-based intra-plant movement, haul road optimisation, equipment upgrades and relocating crushers to lower elevations to cut cost per tonne|Logistics transformation through rail infrastructure investment to reduce historical dependence on road-based dispatches, supported by the Integrated Logistics Management System (ILMS), a Logistics Control Tower with ~95% of dispatches GPS-tracked, and depot realignment to demand centres|Supply chain intelligence via the Blue Yonder platform, evolving from monthly demand planning to a 10-day planning cycle and progressing to dynamic optimisation over a 3-5 day horizon|Digitalisation, innovation and value-added growth as one of the four imperatives driving manufactured capital|Performance excellence framework with regular benchmarking, monthly reviews, advanced control systems and targeted interventions across the manufacturing network|The Dividend Distribution Policy states that the Company has an uninterrupted and increasing dividend payout track record since 2000-01 and that management is confident of maintaining the same. The yearly dividend outgo is stated to depend on prevalent macroeconomic conditions, the industry-specific scenario and the capital expenditure programme under implementation, while retained earnings, as in the past, shall always be used for the expansion of the business. Distribution in FY26 took the form of an interim dividend of Rs 80 per equity share (to be confirmed at the AGM) plus a proposed final dividend of Rs 70 per equity share. On the funding side, the Company's listed borrowings comprise secured Non-Convertible Debentures listed on BSE and NSE with a 7.80% coupon issued on 26-09-2023 and maturing 26-10-2030, with Axis Trustee Services Limited as debenture trustee; as on 31st March, 2026 there were no unutilised amounts from any issue of securities or long-term borrowings, the borrowed funds having been used for the specific purposes for which they were raised.|Carbon intensity targets: Scope 1 of 0.51 tonnes CO2e per tonne of cementitious material and Scope 2 of 0.005 tCO2 per tonne of cementitious material by 2030; FY26 performance was Scope 1 at 0.553 and Scope 2 at 0.009|Water positivity of more than eight times achieved, cited as evidence of progress on the decarbonisation and circularity journey|RE100 ambition - renewable energy footprint continued to expand during FY 2025-26, lifting the green energy share, alongside increased alternative fuel utilisation, new low-carbon cement capacity and advanced waste heat recovery systems|Zero harm at workplace target for employees and workers; FY26 performance was zero fatalities for employees and permanent workers and 4 fatalities for contract workers|Zero deviation from BIS standards target, with zero cases of deviation reported in FY26|Zero non-compliance target on human rights, with no instances of human rights violations reported at operations|Codes, certifications and standards adopted and mapped to the NGRBC principles: Greenpro Certification - CII, ISO-45001, ILO, ISO 14001, ISO-9001, PAT, VCS, ISO 50001, 24/7 Carbon Free Electricity, RE 100, UNGC Guidelines, GRI Standards and BIS Standard|Community development programmes implemented across all operational locations with spend of Rs 55.76 Crore during FY 2025-26, focused on education, skilling, healthcare and community infrastructure|Timely resolution of customer complaints as a stated commitment, with 100% of customer complaints resolved in a timely manner in FY26|Governance: all nine NGRBC principle policies are Board-approved, translated into procedures and extended to value chain partners; a Board-level CSR and Sustainability Committee guides and reviews sustainability strategy, policies, initiatives and risk framework, and the Managing Director (Mr. Neeraj Akhoury) is the highest authority responsible for implementation and oversight of the Business Responsibility policies|Climate mitigation levers named in the BRSR materiality table: renewable energy adoption, waste heat recovery plants, energy conservation and efficiency measures, increased use of biomass and alternative fuels, and air-cooled condensers in thermal power plants|Low-carbon products positioned as an opportunity - manufacturing blended cement products such as PPC, PSC and CC to address customer requirements while reducing emissions|Stated growth ambition toward more than 80 Million tonnes of capacity, pursued with the stated intent that scale must be matched with balance - strengthening resilience and reducing environmental impact
currentContext.expansion: During 2025-26 Shree Cement completed and commissioned two integrated cement units: Jaitaran, Rajasthan (clinker 3.65 MTPA / cement 3.0 MTPA - clinkerisation unit on 30th September, 2025 and cement mill on 12th November, 2025) and Kodla, Karnataka (clinker 3.65 MTPA / cement 3.5 MTPA - clinkerisation unit on 24th February, 2026 and cement mill on 14th March, 2026). Both units were designed with capacities exceeding 10,000 tonnes per day and were progressively optimised within a fortnight after commissioning. Total cement capacity added in India during the year was 12.90 MTPA (including the wholly-owned subsidiary in India), taking cement production capacity to 69.30 MTPA as of 31st March, 2026 (standalone 63.3 MTPA) from 25.60 MTPA a decade earlier. To further expand capacity, the Board has approved an Integrated Cement Plant with clinker capacity of 0.95 MTPA and cement capacity of 0.99 MTPA at Village Daistong, East Jaintia Hills District, Meghalaya, and the Company is actively pursuing multiple greenfield expansion projects at various stages of development to accelerate capacity build-up. On the power side, total installed power capacity increased to 1,137.5 MW (standalone 1,117.50 MW) with green power - waste heat recovery and renewables - at 634.50 MW; a 22 MW WHRS was added at Jaitaran during the year and a further 12 MW at Kodla was commissioned after the close of 2025-26, with WHRS capacity at 264.5 MW. Downstream, the RMC business reached 26 operational plants as of 31st March, 2026 with 10 commercial RMC plants added during the year, and the Company intends to expand this footprint further. Projects that underwent environmental impact assessment during the year indicate the forward pipeline: an integrated cement plant at Chher Moti, Lakhpat, Kachchh, Gujarat (clinker 2.65 Million TPA, cement 4.57 Million TPA, CPP 25 MW, WHRS 23 MW); the Vidharbha Cement Plant at Warora, Chandrapur, Maharashtra (clinker 1.5 Million TPA, cement 3.5 Million TPA, CPP 20 MW, WHRS 9.5 MW); expansion of the Guntur cement plant in Palnadu, Andhra Pradesh (clinker 2.4 to 4.8 Million TPA, cement 4.0 to 7.0 Million TPA, WHRS 15 to 30 MW); plus limestone blocks at Mohra (Chhattisgarh, 1.5 Million TPA), HPB19 Nagaur (Rajasthan, 5.00 Million), Sandi (Chhattisgarh, 3.64 Million TPA), Kondhala (Maharashtra, 2.25 Million TPA) and expansion of the Kachavaram limestone mine (Andhra Pradesh, 3.6 to 7.2 MTPA), and the Datima coal block in Surajpur, Chhattisgarh (targeted 0.36 Million TPA, peak rated 0.54 Million TPA). Capacity expansion is governed by disciplined site selection focused on proximity to key markets and access to optimal limestone reserves, with limestone auction opportunities monitored to secure high-quality reserves.
currentContext.mdna: The Indian cement industry is witnessing a structurally favourable long-term demand scenario supported by infrastructure development, urbanisation, housing needs and increased formalisation of construction activity|During 2025-26 total industry cement production reached approximately 499 Million tonnes with healthy volume growth of 6.5%-7.5% YoY; overall industry capacity utilisation stood at around 71%|Government's record capital outlay of Rs 11.2 Lakhs Crore in the Union Budget aided rapid execution of the National Infrastructure Pipeline, particularly high-speed rail corridors and expressway/road construction|Housing-led demand bolstered by PMAY-Urban 2.0 and PMAY-Gramin targeting completion of over 8.2 Lakhs houses during 2025-26; tier 1 and tier 2 residential sales above Rs 1 Crore grew 14% YoY|GST reduction on cement from 28% to 18% is expected to act as a massive catalyst improving affordability and supporting volume absorption across residential and infrastructure segments|Notable shift in consumption patterns towards Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC), driven mainly by increasing demand from Ready Mix Concrete players and large construction projects that demand higher early strength|Input costs were largely stable in the first half but rose from the beginning of the second half; geopolitical tensions in West Asia disrupted supply chains, spiking coal, petcoke and packing bag costs - the major impact on production costs would be felt in 2026-27|Demand fundamentals remain strong on continued infrastructure investment in roads, railways, metros, ports and urban development, elevated housing demand and gradual recovery in private real estate and commercial construction; the industry is highly optimistic of a favourable demand scenario continuing|Threats to the favourable outlook: geopolitical events and the forecast of a moderate monsoon|The Ready-Mix Concrete segment in India is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 7%-9% over the medium term, driven by urbanisation, infrastructure-led construction, preference for organised construction solutions and demand for faster project execution|Rapid consolidation and significant capacity additions in the industry may create regional oversupply and intensify competitive dynamics, compressing margins through weaker price realisation and lower utilisation|Energy is one of the largest levers of competitiveness; rising green power share in the mix strengthens both cost efficiency and sustainability performance|Rail investment is expected to deliver substantial freight savings while nearly doubling rail's share in the logistics mix over the next few years

risks.risk: Climate change and decarbonisation imperatives (ESG compliance and sustainability)
risks.note: Strategic/regulatory/ESG risk from rising expectations to cut the carbon footprint, alignment with national and sector decarbonisation pathways, tighter emission norms and expanding disclosure requirements including BRSR; physical climate risks such as heat stress and water scarcity may affect operations. Non-compliance may result in penalties, litigation or production constraints, transition costs and potential levies such as higher mining-related taxes can reduce margins, and ESG underperformance may raise the cost of capital and damage reputation and market access.

risks.risk: Market demand cyclicality and industry consolidation
risks.note: Cement demand is cyclical while rapid consolidation and significant capacity additions may create regional oversupply and intensify competition. Downturns and overcapacity can compress margins through weaker price realisation and lower utilisation; competitive pressure may affect market share and increase logistics costs in oversupplied regions.

Energy is a significant component of manufacturing cost and dependence on coal and petcoke with import exposure creates vulnerability to commodity price movements, currency fluctuations and supply disruptions. Higher fuel and freight costs reduce profitability where they cannot be fully passed through, and supply constraints can affect production continuity, working capital and relative cost competitiveness.

Exposure to inbound and outbound logistics constraints, including imported raw materials such as gypsum and fuels, transport capacity limitations, and disruption from geopolitical events and extreme weather. Raw material shortages and dispatch disruptions may reduce production and impair customer service while raising procurement, freight and inventory-buffer working capital.

Expanded digitalisation increases exposure to cyber-attacks including ransomware and phishing, data breaches and IT/OT disruptions, with rising compliance obligations under India's data protection regime. Potential consequences include production disruption, data loss, regulatory penalties, remediation costs, reputational impact and, in severe cases, safety risks.
Strategic/operational risk flagged by the Board arising from an aging workforce, shortages in core technical roles and rising demand for skills.

BRSR material issue: availability of water is critical for operations and changes in water-related regulations may lead to increased costs and operational challenges; mitigated through water conservation, periodic water audits, rainwater harvesting infrastructure, water reuse systems and use of treated municipal STP water.

risks.risk: Biodiversity, land and community (resettlement and rehabilitation) constraints on expansion
risks.note: BRSR material issues: business expansion activities may face constraints if biodiversity-related regulatory requirements are not complied with, and inadequate handling of resettlement and rehabilitation activities may give rise to community conflicts and reputational risk; mitigated through wildlife conservation plans, avoiding operations in eco-sensitive or high biodiversity areas, afforestation, R&R compliance and livelihood restoration initiatives.

BRSR material issue: failure to comply with applicable laws and regulations could lead to regulatory penalties, legal consequences and reputational damage; mitigated through continuous compliance reviews and internal and external audits.

one-line thesis: Shree Cement pivoted from price-defense to volume-chasing in Q4FY26, delivering 11% YoY volume growth and narrowing the price gap with peers by INR 15-20/bag, though FY27 margins face headwinds from INR 150-200/ton cost inflation (fuel/packaging) linked to Middle East tensions. The company leverages a net cash balance of INR 6,400 Cr to fund measured capex (INR 1,500 Cr guidance) while targeting 80 MTPA capacity by 2029.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 4,732/ton realization (FY26, +3.6% YoY); EBITDA: INR 1,212 Cr (Q4, +34% QoQ), INR 4,222 Cr (FY26, +11% YoY ex-one-off); PAT: Not explicitly broken out in transcript text but implied strong via EBITDA; Order Book: N/A (B2C/B2B spot); Net Debt: Net Cash INR 6,400 Cr (Gross Debt ~INR 1,500 Cr). One-offs: FY26 EBITDA excludes INR 80 Cr one-time impact.
guidance: Revenue Growth: Targeting ~40 MTPA cement volume in FY27; Margin: EBITDA/ton under pressure from INR 150-200/ton cost hike in Q1FY27, no specific margin % guidance; Order Inflow: N/A; Capex: INR 1,500 Cr for FY27 (RMC expansion, railway sidings, Meghalaya prep).
order book & pipeline: Not applicable for cement manufacturer; focus is on sales volume run-rate of 10.56 MT in Q4 (annualized ~40 MT).
segment / subsidiary detail: Domestic Cement: 10.56 MT (Q4), +11% YoY, +25% QoQ; Clinker: Minimal strategic focus; UAE (Union Cement): 11.65 lakh tons (Q4), +9% QoQ, revenue AED 247 Mn (+18% QoQ); RMC: 1.99 lakh cum (Q4), INR 90 Cr revenue, expanding from 26 to 36 plants.
growth verticals / optionality: 80 MTPA target by 2029 (current 69.3 MTPA); Meghalaya integrated plant (0.95 MT clinker/0.99 MT cement) with 600 MT limestone reserves; UAE mill expansion (2.5 MT) by Sep '26; RMC scale-up to 50-55 plants.
margins & cost dynamics: Q4 Fuel Cost: INR 1.60/kcal; Q1FY27 Outlook: INR 1.76-1.80/kcal (+10-12%); Total Cost Inflation Q1FY27: INR 150-200/ton (Fuel + Packaging INR 100/ton + Freight); Clinker Factor: 64.8% (Q4); Green Power: 61% of mix.
capex / expansion: FY27 Guidance: INR 1,500 Cr. Key projects: Meghalaya greenfield (front-ended infra spend), Railway sidings (3-4 sites), RMC plant additions. Long-term view: Slowed aggression to match demand, aiming for 80 MTPA by 2029.
capital allocation: Dividend: INR 150/share (FY26, +36% YoY); Net Cash: INR 6,400 Cr; Strategy: Fund capex via internal accruals (no borrowing in 15 years), potential for accelerated capex if geopolitical situation stabilizes.
risks & watch-items: Middle East conflict prolonging fuel cost inflation (Strait of Hormuz disruptions); Moderate monsoon forecast impacting rural demand; Fly ash availability constraints in North India; Execution risk on Meghalaya incentives (none confirmed yet).
management quality / tone: Pragmatic and disciplined; emphasized 'delivery not proclamation'; shifted from 'value over volume' to balancing both after achieving price parity; cautious on FY27 cost outlook due to geopolitics but confident in long-term 80 MTPA goal.
non-obvious takeaways: Management revealed coal inventory is maintained at >90 days (vs peer 60-75), yet cost impact is immediate due to weighted average accounting; Meghalaya capex appears high (INR 1,800 Cr estimated for phase 1) due to front-ended infrastructure (power/land) for ultimate 4-4.5 MT plan; Fly ash shortage narrative challenged by management citing alternative cementitious materials.
challenges → beneficiaries & losers:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rising fuel costs and logistics inflation squeezing margins across the sector | UltraTech Cement | loser | Med | Larger exposure to imported fuel and pan-India logistics may face similar cost pressures without the same net-cash buffer to absorb volatility. |
| Need for premium pricing power in a commoditized market | Shree Cement Limited | beneficiary | High | Successfully narrowed price gap with leaders while maintaining highest EBITDA/ton in peer group; strong balance sheet allows opportunistic capex. |
| Supply chain disruption in Middle East affecting export markets | Union Cement Company (Subsidiary) | loser | Med | UAE operations faced sales slowdown due to regional tension, though reconstruction demand expected post-ceasefire. |

themes.title: Cement demand & pricing recovery
themes.need: Q1FY27 turned cement from a pricing story into a volume-share-plus-fuel-cost story. ULTRACEMCO grew domestic grey volume +13.1% YoY against an estimated ~7-8% industry, delivered its first Rs 5,000cr+ April-June EBITDA (Rs 5,146cr) with EBITDA/ton held above Rs 1,200, and crossed 200.1 MT domestic capacity a year early - but guided Q2FY27 cost UP ~Rs 130-140/ton and pinned the Rs 1,400/ton consolidated target to Q4FY28. The fuel shock, not price, is the swing factor: JKCEMENT's EBITDA/ton fell to Rs 982 from Rs 1,229 YoY despite +19% grey volume, DALBHARAT flagged pet coke 'surged to nearly $160/t' versus a pre-war $110-115, and NUVOCO defended INR 1,079/ton EBITDA only by cutting petcoke from 37% to 27% of fuel mix in a single quarter. Consolidation is visibly compounding (INDIACEM EBITDA/ton Rs 386->400->509->603 across four quarters; DALBHARAT closed Jaypee at Rs 2,850cr EV with Chunar operational and Rewa on trial within 50 days) even as DALBHARAT slipped its 75mt milestone from FY27 to FY28. SHREECEM/RAMCOCEM/JKLAKSHMI/JSWCEMENT/STARCEMENT/BIRLACORPN ride the same volume + consolidation axis.
themes.driver: Q2FY27 is the guided cost trough - ULTRACEMCO ~Rs 130-140/ton, JKCEMENT ~Rs 150/ton and BIRLACORPN Rs 70-80/ton of incremental cost; then fuel-mix agility (NUVOCO's petcoke swing) and whether DALBHARAT's ~Rs 150/t of procurement savings is really 'permanent, not timing'.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company manufactures and sells clinker, cement and Ready Mix Concrete (RMC), which together account for 95.05% of turnover under NIC codes 2394 and 2395. It operates 6 integrated cement unit locations, 10 grinding unit locations and 26 RMC units in India, supported by captive power including waste heat recovery and renewables. It serves a diverse customer base spanning institutional clients and retail consumers, supplying cement for projects ranging from large-scale infrastructure to individual housing units.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The Indian cement industry is witnessing a structurally favourable long-term demand scenario supported by infrastructure development, urbanisation, housing needs and increased formalisation of construction activity
- During 2025-26 total industry cement production reached approximately 499 Million tonnes with healthy volume growth of 6.5%-7.5% YoY; overall industry capacity utilisation stood at around 71%
- Government's record capital outlay of Rs 11.2 Lakhs Crore in the Union Budget aided rapid execution of the National Infrastructure Pipeline, particularly high-speed rail corridors and expressway/road construction
- Housing-led demand bolstered by PMAY-Urban 2.0 and PMAY-Gramin targeting completion of over 8.2 Lakhs houses during 2025-26; tier 1 and tier 2 residential sales above Rs 1 Crore grew 14% YoY
- GST reduction on cement from 28% to 18% is expected to act as a massive catalyst improving affordability and supporting volume absorption across residential and infrastructure segments
- Notable shift in consumption patterns towards Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC), driven mainly by increasing demand from Ready Mix Concrete players and large construction projects that demand higher early strength
- Input costs were largely stable in the first half but rose from the beginning of the second half; geopolitical tensions in West Asia disrupted supply chains, spiking coal, petcoke and packing bag costs - the major impact on production costs would be felt in 2026-27
- Demand fundamentals remain strong on continued infrastructure investment in roads, railways, metros, ports and urban development, elevated housing demand and gradual recovery in private real estate and commercial construction; the industry is highly optimistic of a favourable demand scenario continuing
- Threats to the favourable outlook: geopolitical events and the forecast of a moderate monsoon
- The Ready-Mix Concrete segment in India is expected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 7%-9% over the medium term, driven by urbanisation, infrastructure-led construction, preference for organised construction solutions and demand for faster project execution
- Rapid consolidation and significant capacity additions in the industry may create regional oversupply and intensify competitive dynamics, compressing margins through weaker price realisation and lower utilisation
- Energy is one of the largest levers of competitiveness; rising green power share in the mix strengthens both cost efficiency and sustainability performance
- Rail investment is expected to deliver substantial freight savings while nearly doubling rail's share in the logistics mix over the next few years

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: During 2025-26 Shree Cement completed and commissioned two integrated cement units: Jaitaran, Rajasthan (clinker 3.65 MTPA / cement 3.0 MTPA - clinkerisation unit on 30th September, 2025 and cement mill on 12th November, 2025) and Kodla, Karnataka (clinker 3.65 MTPA / cement 3.5 MTPA - clinkerisation unit on 24th February, 2026 and cement mill on 14th March, 2026). Both units were designed with capacities exceeding 10,000 tonnes per day and were progressively optimised within a fortnight after commissioning. Total cement capacity added in India during the year was 12.90 MTPA (including the wholly-owned subsidiary in India), taking cement production capacity to 69.30 MTPA as of 31st March, 2026 (standalone 63.3 MTPA) from 25.60 MTPA a decade earlier. To further expand capacity, the Board has approved an Integrated Cement Plant with clinker capacity of 0.95 MTPA and cement capacity of 0.99 MTPA at Village Daistong, East Jaintia Hills District, Meghalaya, and the Company is actively pursuing multiple greenfield expansion projects at various stages of development to accelerate capacity build-up. On the power side, total installed power capacity increased to 1,137.5 MW (standalone 1,117.50 MW) with green power - waste heat recovery and renewables - at 634.50 MW; a 22 MW WHRS was added at Jaitaran during the year and a further 12 MW at Kodla was commissioned after the close of 2025-26, with WHRS capacity at 264.5 MW. Downstream, the RMC business reached 26 operational plants as of 31st March, 2026 with 10 commercial RMC plants added during the year, and the Company intends to expand this footprint further. Projects that underwent environmental impact assessment during the year indicate the forward pipeline: an integrated cement plant at Chher Moti, Lakhpat, Kachchh, Gujarat (clinker 2.65 Million TPA, cement 4.57 Million TPA, CPP 25 MW, WHRS 23 MW); the Vidharbha Cement Plant at Warora, Chandrapur, Maharashtra (clinker 1.5 Million TPA, cement 3.5 Million TPA, CPP 20 MW, WHRS 9.5 MW); expansion of the Guntur cement plant in Palnadu, Andhra Pradesh (clinker 2.4 to 4.8 Million TPA, cement 4.0 to 7.0 Million TPA, WHRS 15 to 30 MW); plus limestone blocks at Mohra (Chhattisgarh, 1.5 Million TPA), HPB19 Nagaur (Rajasthan, 5.00 Million), Sandi (Chhattisgarh, 3.64 Million TPA), Kondhala (Maharashtra, 2.25 Million TPA) and expansion of the Kachavaram limestone mine (Andhra Pradesh, 3.6 to 7.2 MTPA), and the Datima coal block in Surajpur, Chhattisgarh (targeted 0.36 Million TPA, peak rated 0.54 Million TPA). Capacity expansion is governed by disciplined site selection focused on proximity to key markets and access to optimal limestone reserves, with limestone auction opportunities monitored to secure high-quality reserves.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Pragmatic and disciplined; emphasized 'delivery not proclamation'; shifted from 'value over volume' to balancing both after achieving price parity; cautious on FY27 cost outlook due to geopolitics but confident in long-term 80 MTPA goal.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Cost leadership: sustained focus on optimising raw material, energy, logistics and fuel costs means the Company 'is widely recognised as one of the lowest-cost cement producers in the industry'
- Premium product mix: ratio of premium products to total trade sales improved from 14.9% in 2024-25 to 20.8% in 2025-26
- Distribution and brand: continued emphasis on brand building, strengthening and expanding the dealer and distribution network, the 'Club Royal' dealer loyalty programme, IPL franchise sponsorship and an always-on television campaign
- Customer franchise: 71% of revenue from repeat customers and a 91% customer satisfaction score
- Energy self-supply and green power: 634.50 MW green energy capacity and 62.1% share of green electricity in total electricity consumption, supporting cost control
- Scale and integration: capacity built from 25.60 MTPA (31st March, 2016) to 69.30 MTPA (31st March, 2026) alongside power capacity of 1,137.50 MW
- Innovation capability: 5 patents granted, Rs 28.51 Crore total R&D investment and DSIR-approved R&D labs at 4 locations
- Logistics optimisation through demand-aligned dispatch locations, IT-enabled analytics, digital route optimisation and deployment of electric vehicles for cement deliveries

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Middle East conflict prolonging fuel cost inflation (Strait of Hormuz disruptions); Moderate monsoon forecast impacting rural demand; Fly ash availability constraints in North India; Execution risk on Meghalaya incentives (none confirmed yet).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Management revealed coal inventory is maintained at >90 days (vs peer 60-75), yet cost impact is immediate due to weighted average accounting; Meghalaya capex appears high (INR 1,800 Cr estimated for phase 1) due to front-ended infrastructure (power/land) for ultimate 4-4.5 MT plan; Fly ash shortage narrative challenged by management citing alternative cementitious materials.
